name: Beth Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is printed with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five and out to the cows before Tom's even put the kettle on. We've got 60 suckler cows on Hollins Farm, about 70 hectares rented from the county council, with spring barley and a bit of fodder beet for winter. Mornings are feeding, checking, bedding, and in spring it's calving, which is the bit I'm known for.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love a cow that's been in trouble getting up and licking her calf, that never gets old. What wears me out is the money side: the rent comes twice a year, the vet bill comes whenever it likes, and beef prices are set by people who've never stood in a muddy yard. Tom drives the school bus to keep us afloat, and we've less than a month of bills put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like most of the shiny things I've seen come and go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the mart: the machines aren't the problem, the prices are. If AI just saves the supermarkets a bit of time, that's their profit, not ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, but it wouldn't help me sleep. AI was never my worry. My worry is the council letter about the rent review sitting on the kitchen table. That letter is there whether AI is hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going the way we do: calve the 60 cows in March and April and sell the stores at Ashby mart in October. The Ford tractor is 22 years old and needs replacing, but I'd put that off two more years. We'd skip the week at Tom's sister's again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, if I'm honest. It's the same squeeze as now, just without anyone to blame but the usual lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's the usual lot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big buyers and the supermarkets, mainly, and a council that would sell its farms tomorrow if it could. I've been in the union and the tenant farmers' association for 30 years because of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI tools. Would anything make you try one, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Kirsty, my daughter, put something on my phone that answers questions, and I deleted it the same night. I can tell a cow's sick by how she stands, and I don't need a phone to tell me.

say: The real problem is **beef prices**, not machines, and I say so at the mart.
If AI only saves time, the **supermarkets** keep the gain, not farmers like me.
think: My worry is the council's **rent review**, and AI hype changes nothing about it.
With **less than a month** saved, one bad vet bill still sinks us.
do: **Calve** the 60 cows in spring and sell the stores at Ashby mart in October.
Put off replacing the **22-year-old tractor** for two more years.
Skip the family **week away** again to keep the rent money safe.
feel: **Tired** from the same money squeeze, with nothing new to hope for.
S0.quote: AI was never my worry. My worry is the council letter about the rent review sitting on the kitchen table.
fieldNote: Her mood comes from **money**, not technology: the rent review, the thin cushion and low beef prices.
She blames **supermarkets and the council** easily and has 30 years of union membership behind it.
Flat refusal of AI tools; she **deleted an app** her daughter installed the same night.

steps.text: Keep calving the 60 suckler cows and selling stores at Ashby mart
Put off replacing the 22-year-old Ford tractor for two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the offices change and the yard doesn't, mostly. That's how I'd read it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the union branch to watch the offices, not the fields. When the council's estate office and the feed merchant run on software, farmers lose the person on the other end of the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a computer in the council office will decide my rent before a robot ever touches my cows. The land agent, Marcus, is a decent man, and I can argue with him. You can't argue with a program that's been told to squeeze every tenancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my paperwork by hand, with Marcus's help as long as he's there. And I'd push the tenant farmers' association to demand that any rent set by software can be challenged by a person. I'd put that motion forward at the spring meeting myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wary. Like when a new owner buys the farm next door and you don't know yet what sort they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Marcus's job goes and the office is all software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ring and get a menu, and the menu won't know that the north field floods every February. Marcus knows that because he's walked it with me in wellies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you see any change on the farm itself in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The feed merchant would take orders through an app, and the vet's bookings too, I expect. My hands would still do the same jobs. My grandson says that's lucky, but I'm not so sure it's luck when the paper side is where they get you.

say: Tell the union branch to watch the **offices**, where software replaces people.
Farmers lose the **person on the phone** when merchants and councils go digital.
think: A council computer will set my **rent** before any robot reaches my cows.
I can argue with **Marcus**, the land agent, but not with a program.
do: Keep doing farm **paperwork by hand** with the land agent's help.
Put a **motion** at the spring meeting so software-set rents can be challenged by a person.
feel: **Wary**, like waiting to see what a new neighbour is like.
S1.quote: A computer in the council office will decide my rent before a robot ever touches my cows.
fieldNote: She sees the **thinking side** of farming, rents and orders, as where change hits her first.
Trust rests on **people she knows**, like the land agent who walked her fields.
Her response is **collective**: a motion at the tenant farmers' association, not a personal fix.

steps.text: Keep doing the farm paperwork by hand with the land agent
Propose a motion letting tenants challenge software-set rents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's two calving seasons. That's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it loud: this is the time for unions and councils to stand up, not to sell out. I'd put it on the association's page that tenant farms are homes, not just land to be handed to whoever owns the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think the council would sell Hollins Farm or merge it with three others for a robot company by 2031. At 63 I'd have no farm, no house and no savings, and a robot would be calving my cows. Tom's bus route would probably be driverless by then too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd ring every council tenant I know and get us in one room. Then I'd lobby the county councillors to stop selling council farms and give sitting tenants the right to stay in their houses. And I'd ask Kirsty, quietly, whether there'd be room for us if it all went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the night we lost 14 lambs in the snow and there was nothing to be done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kirsty, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, I'm not asking for money, I'm asking for a spare room if the worst happens. She'd say yes straight away, and that's what would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The hands-on robots come three years after the thinking AI here. Does that gap matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. The thinking AI takes the council's planning and the merchant's ordering in 2028, and that's when they'd decide to sell. The robots in 2031 just finish the job they'd already planned.

say: Tenant farms are **homes**, and councils must not hand them to robot owners.
This is the moment for **unions** to stand up, not sell out.
think: The council would likely **sell Hollins Farm** or merge it for a robot firm.
At 63 we'd have no farm, house or **savings**, and Tom's bus job may go too.
do: **Gather** every council tenant she knows in one room within a month.
**Lobby** county councillors to stop selling farms and protect tenants' homes.
Ask daughter **Kirsty** for a spare room if the tenancy goes.
feel: **Sick** and helpless, like losing lambs in a snowstorm.
**Hurt** at the idea of leaning on her daughter.
S2.quote: At 63 I'd have no farm, no house and no savings, and a robot would be calving my cows.
fieldNote: The decision she fears is made by **thinking AI in 2028**, before robots arrive.
Two earners at risk: her tenancy and her partner's **bus route**.
Asking her daughter for help is the **hardest part** for her, harder than the fight.

steps.text: Gather all the county's council tenants in one meeting within a month
Lobby county councillors to stop selling council farms
Ask daughter Kirsty for a spare room if the tenancy ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking part and eight for the robots. Now I'm doing sums in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to fight properly, so let's not waste it. I'd want a retirement scheme for tenant farmers on every candidate's leaflet at the next election.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is just long enough for me to hobble out of the gate before the robots walk in. Robots in 2034 means I'm 66, which is about when the pension starts. But the council's thinking AI arrives in 2031, so the rent and the paperwork change while I'm still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell five extra heifers each autumn instead of keeping them, and that money goes in a separate account that Tom and I don't touch. I'd campaign for a retirement scheme for tenant farmers, so we can leave with a bit of money and somewhere to live. I wouldn't buy a single new machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, but not like the fast one. More like a long winter you know you'll get through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling heifers shrinks the herd. Is that a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. Every heifer I sell is a cow I don't have in three years, so I'm eating my seed corn, as my dad would say. But a cushion matters more at my age than a bigger herd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the day the robots arrive in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand back the keys, I suppose, if the pension's there. I'd want to see who's doing the calving, though. I'd go and check on them like an old nosy neighbour.

say: We have time to **fight properly**, so let's not waste it.
Every candidate should back a **retirement scheme** for tenant farmers.
think: Robots in 2034 land near my **pension age**, so I might just make it.
The council's **thinking AI** in 2031 still changes my rent while I farm.
do: Sell **five extra heifers** each autumn into an account we don't touch.
**Campaign** for a tenant farmer retirement scheme before the next election.
Buy **no new machines** at all over the five years.
feel: **Tight in the chest**, but like a long winter she'll get through.
S3.quote: Five years is just long enough for me to hobble out of the gate before the robots walk in.
fieldNote: Timing matters most: robots at **66** roughly match her pension, so the worst is avoided.
She trades **herd size for cash**, knowing it costs her later.
Still **political**: she wants a scheme, not just personal savings.

steps.text: Sell five extra heifers each autumn into a separate savings account
Campaign for a retirement scheme for tenant farmers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 68 for the thinking AI and 71 for the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse for any government to be caught napping. I'd still be at the union meetings saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years means it's my grandson's problem, and I hate that I feel relieved about it. I can't afford to retire at 66 anyway, so I'd be farming till 68 or 70. The robots aren't my danger in this one; the thin bank account is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming Hollins Farm as long as my knees let me. I'd sell the old Ford when the contractor can do the barley for us, and put that money away. And I'd tell my grandson Josh to learn the robots, not the cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved and guilty at the same time. Mostly tired, because the old money worry hasn't gone anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've spent 30 years saying farmers should stick together, and here I am glad it'll miss me. Josh is 15, and it won't miss him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You told Josh to learn the robots. Isn't that odd, from someone who deleted an app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's odd, I know. It's too late for me, but I'm not daft enough to wish my own stubbornness on a boy of 15.

say: A decade's warning leaves **no excuse** for governments to be caught out.
I'll keep saying it at **union meetings**.
think: Ten years makes it my **grandson's problem**, and I feel guilty for being relieved.
My danger is the **thin bank account**, since I can't afford to retire at 66.
do: **Keep farming** Hollins Farm until 68 or 70, as long as her knees allow.
Sell the **old Ford tractor** once a contractor does the barley, and save the money.
feel: **Tired**, because the old money worry stays.
S4.quote: Ten years means it's my grandson's problem, and I hate that I feel relieved about it.
fieldNote: With time on her side, her worry falls back to the **pre-existing** one: no savings to retire on.
Real **contradiction**: refuses AI herself but tells her grandson to learn robots.
Her **solidarity** makes the relief feel like a betrayal to her.

steps.text: Keep farming Hollins Farm until 68 or 70
Sell the old Ford tractor and bank the money for retirement

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because the council would decide before any of us could organise. What would help is a law that a tenant keeps the right to live in the farmhouse, and a proper retirement scheme for tenant farmers, so leaving doesn't mean leaving with nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. I've pulled calves out backwards in the dark for thirty years, and nobody is going to teach a machine to care about that cow. Maybe it'll do the job, but it won't care, and somebody should write that down.

headlineQuote: I've pulled calves out backwards in the dark for thirty years, and nobody is going to teach a machine to care about that cow.
portrait: Beth, 58, farms **60 suckler cows** and barley on a council tenancy with less than a month saved.
A lifelong **union and association** member, she blames supermarkets, buyers and a council keen to sell farms.
She refuses **AI tools** outright and sees the threat arriving through rents and offices first.
Her mood tracks **timing**: alarmed at two years, back to old money worries at ten.
She'd **organise and lobby** before acting alone, and only reluctantly lean on her daughter.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the council would sell or merge her tenancy before tenants could organise.
whatWouldHelp: A law letting tenants **keep the farmhouse**, plus a retirement scheme for tenant farmers.
